gap: No result ChatGPT got states how many amps each unit can deliver at 240 V. Rated watts ÷ 240 V works out to 16.0 A for the BLUETTI Apex 300, 16.7 A for the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3, 25 A for the Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus (Anker prints '25A Max') and 30 A for the Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus and EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra. So the Apex 300's 50 A-labelled NEMA 14-50R outlet supplies at most 32% of its label.
standout_why: I opened Watt & Warden (cited) and Power Station Field Guide (cited) and asked each what the page itself prints. Watt & Warden prints 240 V watts and weights, but no amps at 240 V, no cost per kWh and no Wh per lb. It also lists a NEMA 14-50 on the F3800 Plus, but Anker's own spec sheet lists only a TT-30 and an L14-30R. Power Station Field Guide does not state amps at 240 V or prices. SolarGenReview's EV article and Outbound Power returned HTTP 429, so I could not check them. ChatGPT's own answers gave watts and minutes at 3,000 W, never amps at 240 V. Its only amps remark was that a 20 A, 240 V appliance can draw 4,800 W.
decides: Shoppers size a 240 V appliance by its circuit amps, so the pick depends on amps at 240 V, not on which outlet the unit has. The Apex 300 (16.0 A) and DELTA Pro 3 (16.7 A) cannot carry a 240 V load above about 16 A, even though each has a 30 A or 50 A outlet. Loads from 16.7 A up to 25 A need the F3800 Plus or a bigger unit, and loads up to 30 A need the Explorer 5000 Plus or the DELTA Pro Ultra. Above 30 A, only the DELTA Pro Ultra X bundle (50 A) does it from one inverter. This makes the Apex 300 the cheapest single-box route only for 240 V loads of 16 A or less. At $1,499 it costs $93.69 per 240 V amp, against $123.30 for the DELTA Pro Ultra.
